tip: For 'I have been studying', Hindi uses the present continuous plus से (se = since): तीन महीने से हिंदी पढ़ रहा हूँ (teen mahine se hindi parh raha hoon).
One doctor, plural verb: respect turns देख रहा है (dekh raha hai) into देख रहे हैं (dekh rahe hain). Elders, doctors and bosses get the plural form even when they're one person.
English -ing never changes, but रही (rahi) does: Shobha gets दौड़ रही है (daud rahi hai) because she's female – a man would be दौड़ रहा है (daud raha hai).
You wait OF the bus, not for it: बस का इंतज़ार कर रहा हूँ (bus ka intezaar kar raha hoon = doing the bus's wait). इंतज़ार (intezaar) always takes का.
Phone Hindi skips 'this is' – you say who you are directly: मैं डॉक्टर शर्मा बोल रहा हूँ (main Doctor Sharma bol raha hoon = I am Doctor Sharma speaking).
No dummy 'it' for weather – rain and drizzle just happen: बूँदा-बाँदी हो रही है (boonda-baandi ho rahi hai = drizzle is happening).
उड़ाना (udana) means 'make fly': kids are पतंग उड़ा रहे हैं (patang uda rahe hain), making the kite fly. Plain उड़ना (udna) is what the kite itself does.
चार्ज हो रहा है (charge ho raha hai) = 'is getting charged' – हो (ho) for things happening on their own. If YOU charge it, that's चार्ज कर रहा हूँ (charge kar raha hoon).
फ़ोन करता हूँ (phone karta hoon) looks like 'I call' but means 'I'll call' – the simple present works as a right-away promise in Hindi.
'Can you understand' uses पाना: समझ पा रहे हैं (samajh paa rahe hain = managing to understand). पाना (paana) after a verb means 'manage to, succeed in'.
Doubling जैसे-जैसे (jaise-jaise) means 'as... steadily': जैसे-जैसे शहर बढ़ रहा है (jaise-jaise shahar barh raha hai) = as the city keeps growing.
मिलना (milna) means both 'meet' and 'get'. Here मिल रहे हैं (mil rahe hain) = we're meeting; but पानी मिल रहा है (paani mil raha hai) would mean water is available.
करवाओ (karvao) = have it done by someone else: जाँच नियमित करवाओ (jaanch niyamit karvao) = get the check-up done regularly. Doing it yourself would be करो (karo).
No verb 'to need' – the needed thing is the subject: बक्सा चाहिए (baksa chahiye = a box is needed). The person who needs it takes को (ko).
छाता ले लो (chhata le lo): the extra लो (lo) marks doing it for yourself. दे दो (de do) would mark doing it for someone else. Hindi tags who benefits.
A number plus -ों makes 'all of them': चारों बच्चे (chaaron bachche) = all four children, दोनों (donon) = both. English needs the extra word 'all'.
Hindi chains actions with -कर (kar = having done): बिछाकर बैठो (bichhakar baitho) = having spread it, sit. English says 'lay it out AND sit' – Hindi drops the 'and'.
One little ना (na) does all of English's tag questions: सब ठीक है ना? (sab theek hai na?) covers 'isn't it', 'right?', 'aren't you' – no matching verb needed.
लग रहा है (lag raha hai) = 'is looking, seeming': चेहरा उतरा लग रहा है (chehra utra lag raha hai) = your face seems drawn. लगना (lagna) covers impressions.
'Is sitting' is NOT बैठ रहे (baith rahe) – that means in the act of sitting down. The seated state uses बैठे (baithe): बैठे अख़बार पढ़ रहे हैं (baithe akhbaar parh rahe hain) = seated, reading.
वाला (vala) turns a noun into 'the one with it': ऑटो वाले ने (auto vale ne) = the auto guy did. Same trick everywhere – चाय वाला (chai vala) = the tea seller.
-इए is the respectful command: धीरे बोलिए (dheere boliye = please speak slowly). बोलो (bolo) is the plain version you'd use with friends.
